description:
We’re two seniors at MCA, an international high school in South Korea, who want to use NASA data and engineering to tackle real Earth science problems.

Together, we combine environmental data analysis with hardware and communications. This lets us design solutions that go beyond the screen, from sensor-based monitoring to tools that help communities respond to environmental change.
summary: Imagine farming the same land for twenty years, then watching the seasons stop behaving the way you learned. For a farmer, a wrong crop choice isn’t just a bad harvest. It’s a year of work and income at risk, which is hard to bear when farming is already economically tough. That’s why we built FieldShift, a web app that helps farmers in South Korea ask: does my usual crop still fit my weather? A user picks a region, and the app pulls real NASA POWER data for that spot, including temperature, rainfall, and sunlight. It then compares the current crop with alternative crop rotation strategies and shows which ones match the local climate best. This answers the Field Shift challenge by turning NASA Earth observations into a simple decision-support tool for adapting farms. It matters because most farmers never see this data, and FieldShift makes it easy to use and honest about its limits.
details:
FieldShift helps farmers in South Korea answer a simple question: which crop rotations fit my local climate best? A user chooses a province and a city or county from a national list of Korean regions. The app sends that location’s coordinates to the NASA POWER API and gets back daily temperature, rainfall and sunlight for 2025, then turns it into monthly tables and charts that are easy to read. It checks how many days fall inside each crop’s ideal temperature range and averages those scores for each rotation strategy. The results appear as side-by-side cards, a chart, and a short message about which strategy fits best.

The main beneficiaries are farmers and agricultural advisers who can get a quick, local look at how well different crops match the climate, without needing a science background. NASA data becomes a plain comparison instead of a spreadsheet of daily numbers. We want to help farmers make better-informed choices as the climate changes, and we see FieldShift as a starting point for planning that works alongside expert advice. We hope it can grow into a tool that supports resilient farming across Korea.

We built it with Python and Streamlit for the web interface, pandas for data analysis, and the requests library to call the NASA POWER API. Our region, crop, and rotation information is stored in CSV files, and we used GitHub to share our code. We also used Claude, an AI assistant, to help debug and test some of the code.

Since everyone had access to the same data, we focused on making it useful for a real farmer. FieldShift turns raw daily climate data into a simple comparison of crop rotation strategies, shown as clear cards and charts that anyone can read, and we chose to be upfront about what the app can’t tell you instead of overstating its results.

We handled missing NASA values so they wouldn’t distort the results. Each region uses one representative coordinate, so results may differ from a real field, and we use only one year of data, so a longer record would show climate trends better. Right now we only score temperature, and our rainfall thresholds are placeholders, so we say clearly that the app doesn’t predict harvests. Our crop and rotation data are prototype candidates that experts should verify. Next, we plan to check them with agricultural experts, add soil moisture, rainfall comparison, heat and drought risk, and let farmers set their own priorities.
projectRefs: Inquiry for data on the light saturation point (LX) and optimal and maximum temperatures of major crops (horticulture, wild vegetables, medicinal, food, and recent tropical crops)
